findings.title: Successful cleanup emits unconditional error-level logs
findings.body: The new cleanup logging uses Error for normal batch selection and successful deletion, including empty batches with a nil error. The same issue occurs in both annotation cleanup branches. Orphan-tag cleanup therefore emits error messages even when there is nothing to clean, on every scheduled run. This creates false failure signals for log-based monitoring and logs entire ID batches at the normal production log level. Use debug-level logging for successful work and error-level logging only for actual failures.

findings.title: SQLite ID-list construction has quadratic allocation cost
findings.body: Each iteration formats and copies the entire accumulated ID list into a new string. For a batch of N IDs, this makes construction quadratic rather than linear and can allocate gigabytes of temporary strings for batches around the newly tested size of 32,767. This is a substantial regression from the previous database-side subquery and can make large SQLite cleanup batches consume excessive CPU and memory. Build the list with a strings.Builder or a byte buffer instead.

findings.title: Large cleanup batches exceed MySQL and PostgreSQL parameter limits
findings.body: The non-SQLite path now creates one bound parameter per selected ID without limiting the number of parameters. MySQL prepared statements and PostgreSQL's bind protocol have a 65,535-parameter limit, so a configured cleanup batch larger than that fails whenever enough eligible rows are present. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not have this restriction. Split deletion into parameter-limit-safe chunks or use an integer-literal strategy for these dialects as well, so previously working large batch configurations continue to clean annotations and orphaned tags.
